Question #4: Is typeof() ever different from class() and from mode() for the same object? Look at your results above and explain any case where this happens (or, if you did not see one, explain what you would expect for a matrix or factor).
Answer: Yes, typeof(), class(), and mode() can be completely different for the same object

Question #5: When you ran the conversion-fail chunk, R produced NA and a warning instead of stopping with an error.

Why do you think R is designed to give a warning here rather than crashing the whole script?
(i think R is designed to give a warning because R is designed primiraly for data analysis)



What are the risks of this behavior if you don’t read your warnings?
(if you ignore the warnings, you may unknowingly perform analysis on a dataset that contains missing values(NA))



Question #6: as.logical(0) and as.logical(1) convert to FALSE and TRUE.

What do you think as.logical(2) and as.logical(-1)` will produce?
(both will produce TRUE)


```{r}
logicalplus <- as.logical(2)
logicalminus <- as.logical(-1)
print(logicalplus)
print(logicalminus)
```

Test it, then explain the rule R seems to be following.
(when coercing numeric values to logical values in R exactly 0 coverts to false while any non zero numbers whether positive or negative converts to true)

Question #7: paste() and paste0() produced different results for the same two strings. Explain exactly why, referencing what each function does by default.

(paste() and paste0() produce different results because they use different default separators (sep) to join strings.
)

Question #9: Some programming languages automatically convert "5" + 5 into 10 without an error. R does not.

Based on what you’ve learned about R’s data types in this lab, why do you think R requires an explicit conversion instead of guessing what the programmer meant?
(R needs a conversion because "5" is text, not a number. Using as.numeric() changes it into a number so R can add it to 5.)



Question #10: Suppose a classmate writes a script that reads a column of “numbers” from a text file. The column looks numeric, but when they try sum() on it, R throws an error. Based on everything in this lab (types, typeof()/class()/mode(), conversion, warnings), write a short paragraph explaining what likely went wrong and the steps you’d take to diagnose and fix it.

(The numbers might have been read as text instead of numeric values. I would check the data type using class() and look at the values using head(). Then I would use as.numeric() to convert them into numbers. I would also check for errors or missing values before using sum() again.


Conclusion
In 3–4 sentences, summarize what you learned about how R handles different data types, and why understanding typeof()/class() and conversion functions matters before doing arithmetic or combining data.

(I learned that R has different data types, such as numbers, characters, and logical values. The `typeof()` and `class()` functions help me check the type of data I am working with. I also learned that conversion functions like `as.numeric()` can change text into numbers when needed. Understanding data types helps avoid errors when doing calculations or combining data.)
